entries.title: raddle: codeguide's woven-in successor
entries.brief: Docs regenerated once at merge time over the plan's diff, folded into Finalize's contract; the geometry and the parallel-regeneration design exist
entries.body:
From `manifest/roadmap.md` Someday.
raddle is codeguide's woven-in successor.
A parallel-regeneration design exists.
It folds into `Finalize`'s own contract rather than a separate producer, since `Shed` has no slots for it to occupy.

## Design

> **Status: Design partially exists, not scheduled.** Deprioritized — not required to land a first `loom` plan. Raddle-regeneration is folded into `Finalize`'s own contract, not a reserved phase slot of its own (see `contracts/recipes/loom-recipe.yaml`). This doc covers the parts of raddle's design settled during the vacation-time discussion, not the whole module.

## What it is

Raddle is codeguide's weaving-vocabulary successor, living in `weft`: it generates docs over the diff a plan produced, building heavily on Millhouse's `codeguide-update`, deliberately not the implementer's job — implementers, busy with code, forget the docs.
See When it runs below for when regeneration actually happens.

## Geometry — where raddle content lives

Every raddle file lives under `_lyx/raddle/` inside each worktree, mirroring that worktree's own code tree.
It is resolved by plain path lookup joined onto the anchor path, with no junction of its own and no hub-level presence at all.
It reaches the weft through the already-wired `_lyx` junction, like every other `_lyx` subtree.

`_raddle` is **not** a reserved hub name and is never junction-reached.

Raddle content is tracked `_lyx` content and therefore needs no `.lyx` mirror, per the Durable-vs-Ephemeral State Invariant.

This section records the geometry only — raddle's actual implementation, including the shadow tree's path-lookup code and any accessor, is explicitly out of scope here.

## Parallel regeneration — unlike card implementation, this is safe

Unlike webster's card implementation (which needs real worktree isolation for safe parallelism — see webster-parallel-execution.md), raddle's doc regeneration can safely run as **parallel forks**, for reasons specific to what raddle does:

1. **No per-fork git commit needed mid-flight.**
   Card parallelism failed partly because concurrent `git add`+commit from multiple forks race on the same git index.
   Raddle forks don't need this — each fork writes its own module doc to disk;
   **one combining commit** happens at the end (`fabric.SyncWeft(...)`, see `internal/fabricengine`), covering all raddle changes at once.
   This eliminates the git-index race entirely.
2. **Raddle only reads code, never writes it.**
   Card forks editing code concurrently risked seeing each other's unstable, half-finished intermediate states.
   Raddle forks read an already-landed, stable code state — no "who sees what when" problem.
3. **True file-disjointness is easy to guarantee.**
   With a clean module → doc mapping (one changed module → one raddle `.md` file), there's no ambiguity about who writes where, unlike card `changes-files` declarations which could turn out wrong after the fact.

**Structure:** parallel leaf forks (one per changed module, no dependencies between them) → one final step regenerating any top-level summary (`Overview.md`) from the now-updated module docs (must wait for all leaves) → one combined `fabric.SyncWeft(...)` commit covering everything.

**No race on `Overview.md`:** the "must wait for all leaves" sequencing above prevents concurrent writers to `Overview.md` within one regeneration run — it's a single, serial final step, never touched by the leaf forks themselves.
No additional lock needed there.

## When it runs: deferred to merge-time, not mid-task

Regenerating raddle is token-heavy and takes real wall-clock time, so it should run **once**, not twice.
Running it right after Webster (against the task's own fork-point) and then again at actual merge (against parent's real, possibly-since-moved HEAD) would do exactly that: two regenerations, the first thrown away the moment parent has advanced.

**Decision: raddle regenerates once, at merge-time, against parent's actual current HEAD** — not mid-task.
This collapses the two potential runs into one and guarantees the output describes the real merge result, not a stale fork-point.

**Consequence for the merge lock:** the lock protecting this step must span the **entire** critical section — read parent's current HEAD, run the leaf-fork + `Overview.md` regeneration against it, commit via `SyncWeft` — as one atomic unit, not just around the final git write.
If another task's merge landed in parent partway through regeneration, the docs would be stale against the HEAD they're about to be committed onto.
Same "advance only on confirmed success" discipline the `Warp-SHA` trailer mechanism uses elsewhere in `fabric` for recording a baseline, extended to cover the compute step, not just the write step.

**Decided:** raddle has no reserved phase slot of its own in loom's producer list (`contracts/recipes/loom-recipe.yaml`) — regeneration is folded into `Finalize`'s own contract instead, landed in `internal/landingshed`.
See internal/landingshed for Finalize's side of the contract.

## Staleness tracking, via `fabric`

Raddle's snapshot files describe the codebase as of some SHA, and only get regenerated by an explicit, separate command — they can silently drift out of date as cards land.
Using `fabric`'s Warp-SHA trailer mechanism (see `internal/fabricengine`):

- Raddle's regeneration command records its baseline by passing `snapshotTags=["raddle"]` to `Fabric.Commit`, alongside whatever raddle files the regeneration produced.
  **The warp SHA recorded should be the warp code SHA raddle describes — the last warp commit *before* the regeneration — not raddle's own resulting weft commit SHA**, otherwise later staleness checks compute against the wrong baseline;
  the `Warp-SHA` trailer holds exactly that value, so the trailer form satisfies this requirement naturally.
- A regeneration that finds the codebase unchanged since its last recorded baseline still needs to advance that baseline, even though it produces no weft content — this is exactly the case that motivated the empty-commit rule (see the tags-force-a-weft-commit Shared Decision in `internal/fabricengine`): tagging a `Commit` call with `snapshotTags=["raddle"]` and no changed files still lands an empty weft commit carrying the baseline, so a no-op regeneration advances the baseline instead of reporting drift forever.
- A staleness check is the **three-step** idiom `Fabric.SnapshotWarpSHA`'s own doc comment specifies, not the naive two-step composition: read the baseline via `SnapshotWarpSHA("raddle")`, confirm it still resolves via `f.Warp.SHAExists`, and only then call `f.Warp.ChangedFilesSince` to get a precise answer — *"raddle's map is N commits behind current HEAD, covering these files"* — instead of a vague, always-true warning that raddle "might" be outdated.
  Skipping the `SHAExists` check and calling `ChangedFilesSince` directly hard-errors on a warp SHA a rebase has since rewritten, exactly the case this mechanism exists to survive: the check lets a post-rebase raddle regenerate cleanly instead.

## Boundary with quarry (deliberately not coupled)

- **quarry** only cares about source code files, never markdown, and has **no knowledge of raddle whatsoever**.
- **Raddle never modifies code and therefore has no reason to notify quarry** — that coupling was proposed once during design and correctly rejected.
  Raddle's own use of `fabric` is purely for its own staleness tracking, unrelated to quarry.
- Both consumers independently depend on `fabric`;
  they do not depend on each other.

## What Master must know about raddle content (see `internal/websterengine`'s package documentation)

Raddle files are a **snapshot** of the codebase from *before* a plan started — they are only regenerated by a separate, explicit command, not continuously.
Master (and any fork inheriting its context) must treat raddle content as "how things were before this plan," never outranking a fresh quarry query or an actual file read once cards have started landing.

## Related

- `internal/fabricengine` — the `Warp-SHA`/`Snapshot` trailer and `SyncWeft` mechanics this design relies on.
- `contracts/recipes/loom-recipe.yaml` — the flat producer list Raddle has no slot of its own in;
  regeneration is folded into `Finalize`'s contract instead.
- The `internal/boardengine` package documentation — `PATTERN.md` (raddle's neighbor in `weft`) mentioned there.

entries.title: webster: worktree-per-card parallel execution
entries.brief: Give each DAG-independent group its own fabric-spawned worktree so concurrent cards stop sharing one git index; parked until measured evidence says it pays
entries.body:
From `manifest/roadmap.md` Someday.
Give each DAG-independent group its own `fabric`-spawned worktree, so concurrent cards stop sharing one git index.
A speed optimization over an already-correct sequential system.
The loom plan spec and `internal/websterengine`'s package documentation describe the sequential model it would extend.

## Design

> **Status: parked, not rejected — one shape was rejected, a second is open.** What two explorations rejected is *concurrent forks inside one working tree*, which race on a single shared git index; the 2026-08-20 worktree-per-group shape below does not share that index and is not covered by that rejection. Read past this banner before concluding the idea is dead — the earlier wording said "rejected for now both times" and, until the 2026-08-29 designs audit, sent readers away before the open shape, the measured case study, and the decision gate.
> Still parked, though one of its original three reasons has since fallen: the **Adopt quarry's glyph alphabet as the plan alphabet** item shipped (`go.mod` now requires `github.com/Knatte18/quarry`), so the DAG source this doc used to wait on exists. What still parks it: it is a speed optimization over an already-correct sequential system, and webster's landed card-list rewrite (`internal/websterengine`) should get real running mileage first. Reopen it on the measured evidence the Decision gate section names, never on estimate.
> Per the documentation lifecycle, if this is ever picked up the durable parts fold into `internal/websterengine`'s package doc and this file is deleted; if abandoned, this file is simply deleted.

## Why it's parked

loom-plan-spec.md is deliberately a flat, sequential card list with **no DAG wired into scheduling**.
Running cards as *parallel* forks would require reintroducing a DAG and worktree isolation, which reopens exactly the problem sequential execution avoids: git's index/staging area is a single shared file per working tree, so two forks concurrently committing — even to fully disjoint files — race on the same lock.
Current (2026) ecosystem guidance treats worktree isolation as effectively required for concurrent subagents on the same repo.
A declared-disjoint card pair that turns out (via deviation) to actually overlap is a **live corruption risk** in a concurrent-no-worktree model, not just a bookkeeping problem to fix after the fact as it is sequentially;
quarry would also see other forks' uncommitted, potentially syntactically-broken in-flight edits while serving a concurrent fork's query, since there's no filesystem isolation between them.

**A possible middle ground, if revisited:** let forks edit concurrently (the LLM-thinking-dominated part) but serialize the actual `git add`+commit+verify step through a mutex in webster's Go orchestration ("edit in parallel, land sequentially").
Even this requires *strictly enforced* file-disjointness (not just DAG-edge-absence) to be safe.
Not built.

## A possible unblocking shape (2026-08-20)

A structural alternative to the rejected concurrent-forks-in-one-tree shape above: each DAG-independent group (a batch, possibly one card) gets its own `fabric`-spawned worktree — genuinely its own git index/HEAD, which is what the rejected shape lacked — running the existing `Preflight → Webster → Finalize` row set unchanged, with `Webster`'s `Geometry.PlanDir` (already told, not derived) pointed at the source plan and a new batch-filter selecting the one group to run.
Merge-back reuses `fabric`'s existing merge machinery, not new infrastructure, and a group's completion gates on a build+test of the *merged* result rather than of the group's own worktree in isolation.
The ready set recomputes wave to wave rather than being precomputed upfront, so a group that turns out to depend on another's output is simply not ready yet instead of being mis-scheduled.

This shape is what makes the rejection at the top of this doc specific rather than general: that rejection was about concurrent forks sharing one checkout's git index, which worktree-per-group does not do.

Grouping granularity (one card vs. several) is orthogonal to safety — the original rejection above conflated it with the working-tree-sharing hazard, but genuine worktree-per-lane isolation is what actually matters.
Not yet a plan: the DAG source exists now that the **Adopt quarry's glyph alphabet as the plan alphabet** item has shipped,
but it still needs a writeup reconciling this with the still-open questions elsewhere in this doc (typical-plan wave-width evidence, the batchifier/planner change needed to emit groups).

The per-lane mechanics have since shipped elsewhere: batten's recipe (create, seed, run, teardown as ordinary producers) and its run-id addressing carry N concurrent lane runs side by side, so a lane is a batten-style run whose child seed names a webster-lane recipe — none of that machinery is this item's to build.
What remains genuinely webster's: the wave scheduler (event-driven, recomputing the ready set on each lane's merge-back — never a continuously maintained DAG), the plan group-filter, and a non-forking webster variant.
That last one is the real structural change: today's webster runs forks inside the Master session's own context, which binds execution to one session in one worktree;
a lane needs agents spawned into the lane worktree's own reed session instead, scoped to just that lane's group.

## The case study (from an earlier, more detailed design draft, `websterv2.md`, now retired)

A card-level dependency analysis of the 42-card plan that built webster v1 overturned the naive "linear chain" assumption:

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Cards | 42 |
| Batches (sequential) | 9 |
| True card-DAG depth (critical path) | 7 |
| Peak wave width | 10 |
| Cards off the critical path | 83% (35 of 42) |
| Wave widths (1→7) | 10, 9, 7, 7, 6, 2, 1 |

- **The batch DAG over-constrains.**
  Sequential batching's own dependency declarations were largely spurious at card granularity — ~26 cards (waves 1–3) could have run as three parallel waves instead of spread across four sequential batches.
- **File-conflicts barely bind** when the plan is create-then-extend — nearly every file-conflict pair is already dependency-ordered into different waves.
- **The tail is the real ceiling, not dependencies** — a hard funnel near the end of a plan (e.g. final registration → sandbox validation) crashes wave widths regardless of fork budget;
  speedup is front-loaded.
- **Honest speedup estimate: ~2–3× wall-clock**, discounted from a naively-computed 3–5× because a wave's wall-clock is its *slowest* card,
  and the heaviest implementation cards tend to sit on the critical path.
  Two caveats push it down further: semantic edges were *inferred* from card descriptions (real edit-time dependencies only add edges and shrink waves), and 42 cards is an atypically large plan — a routine 5–10-card task has little fan-out headroom and would show a speedup near 1×, dominated by warm-context, not parallelism.

## Decision gate, if ever revisited

Run the card-DAG width analysis across several *real* completed plans, weighted for **typical** task size, not this one outlier.
Wide (fat waves, short critical path, low file-conflict) → an executor might pay off.
Narrow (long critical path, most cards chained, or simply few cards) → parallelism won't materialize;
sequential is the complete correct design, not just the MVP.

## The separable, cheap win already taken

A planner that emits true card dependencies (`depends-on`) instead of an over-constrained batch line recovers most of the *width* insight with **no worktrees and no concurrent execution** — this is exactly what loom-plan-spec.md already does.
Only the *executor that actually runs the width* (this entry) remains parked.

## Relationship to quarry (Part B of the retired draft)

The retired `websterv2.md` draft also had a Part B — structured impact lookup via `go/packages`/`gopls` (find-all-references as a Go verb instead of LLM-driven grep).
That idea is superseded, not lost: it's the direct ancestor of [quarry](https://github.com/Knatte18/quarry), which generalizes it to a multi-language, daemon-based design.

## Related

- `internal/websterengine`'s package documentation — the sequential model this would extend.
- loom-plan-spec.md — already captures the cheap win (`depends-on`).
- [quarry](https://github.com/Knatte18/quarry) — Part B's successor.

entries.title: reed: cross-worktree columns, own-window anchoring, per-window attach
entries.brief: Three related ideas for reed beyond one pane per strand and one window per worktree
entries.body:
From `manifest/roadmap.md` Someday, three items kept together:
- **reed: cross-worktree columns.** All worktrees in one tmux window, a column per worktree; needs a name for the new per-worktree grouping layer this introduces and a column-count/fallback policy.
- **reed: own-window strand anchoring.** A `display` anchor that spawns a strand into its own switchable tmux window instead of a pane.
- **reed: independent per-window attach via tmux session groups.** tmux's session-groups feature would let multiple `lyx reed attach` invocations show different windows independently, instead of sharing one today.

## Design

> Three related, not-yet-scoped ideas about reed outgrowing "one pane per strand, one window per worktree." Grouped here because each is a candidate building block for the others.

## Cross-worktree columns

All worktrees in one tmux window, a column per worktree.

Needs its own name for the per-worktree grouping layer this introduces — it cannot be called "session": that's already tmux's own term, and already 1:1 with a worktree in reed's plumbing today. Also needs a decision on how many columns fit before falling back to tmux windows-as-pages.

Candidate group-layer names surveyed so far and still free: **Heddle, Batten, Bobbin, Sley**. Already taken elsewhere in this codebase: Warp, Weft, Shuttle, Treadle, Shed, Loom, Reed, Strand, Fabric, Quarry, Crucible, and Selvage (claimed by the shipped header-replacement work — see `internal/reedengine`'s `selvagepane.go`).

## Own-window strand anchoring

A `display` anchor that spawns a strand into its own switchable tmux window instead of a pane.

## Independent per-window attach via tmux session groups

Today two `lyx reed attach` invocations join the same tmux session object — a shared "current window" pointer, and mismatched terminal sizes fighting over layout.

tmux's session-groups feature (`new-session -t <existing-session>`) would let each invocation show a different window independently, which reed's `attach` verb does not use today. This is a candidate building block for both ideas above, likely exposed as something like an `--window <n>` flag, or hidden entirely behind one verb that spawns the needed loose terminal windows automatically.

## Operator, 2026-10-05: strands in depth, not stacked in height

Two strands stacked as panes in one window are unreadable on a small laptop screen.
Stack them in depth instead: one tmux window per strand, behaving like tabs within the run's terminal window.

- The driver always lives in window 0, with its `loom-status` strand beside it.
- Each agent the driver spawns (Discussion-Write, a Burler round, Webster's Master) gets its own window, named by its role, so the tmux status line lists what runs.
- The window closes when the agent ends, and the view falls back to the driver.
- **No focus stealing.** A new window must never pull focus away from a window the operator is typing in; an automatic switch on spawn is unwanted for that reason.
  Open: how a new window announces itself instead (status-line highlight, tmux activity flag, a switch only when the current window is idle), and whether tmux session groups are needed so each attached terminal keeps its own current window.

## Related

- `internal/reedengine`'s package documentation — the shipped work that claims the "Selvage" name; reed still has no window support today.

entries.title: warp-visibility: CLAUDE.local.md invisible in the Fabric repo's git history
entries.brief: Expose CLAUDE.local.md by symlink so nothing lyx-related shows in the Fabric repo's history; the constraints half is out of date
entries.body:
From `manifest/roadmap.md` Someday.
Expose `CLAUDE.local.md` via symlink (Windows-Developer-Mode note and a copy fallback), so nothing lyx-related shows up in the Fabric repo's own git history.

Out of date as of 2026-10-04: the design below and the roadmap line say the `CONSTRAINTS.md`-equivalent half is covered because `PATTERN.md` lives in weft.
After `pattern-init`, `PATTERN.md` sits at the repo root and is tracked in the warp repo, so that half is not covered; decide it afresh when this is picked up.
The ignore entry for `CLAUDE.local.md` goes to `.git/info/exclude` through `fabricengine`, never a tracked `.gitignore` (the Fabric Git entry, `PATTERN-fabric-git`).

## Design

> **Status: Design — not built.** Split out from `internal/fabricengine` — the vacation-time discussion bundled this into the Fabric cutover step opportunistically ("we're touching that area anyway"), but the mechanism itself is filesystem-linking/worktree setup, not git coordination — it doesn't depend on `fabric`'s own architecture (`gitrepo`, `SyncWeft`, `RevertWithWeft`) at all. Per the documentation lifecycle, durable parts fold into whichever package ends up owning worktree setup (`warp`/`fabric`'s topology side, or `loom`'s init step) when this lands, and this file is deleted.
>
> **Scope reduced (2026-07):** the `CONSTRAINTS.md`-equivalent half of this task is superseded by the `PATTERN.md` item — `PATTERN.md` lives in `weft`, already invisible to the Fabric repo, so there is no constraints directory left to hide. This task now covers only `CLAUDE.local.md`.

## Design principle

Nothing lyx-related should be visible in the Fabric repo's own git history — everything lives in `weft`.

## `CONSTRAINTS.md`-equivalent — superseded by `PATTERN.md`

**No longer this task's concern.** `PATTERN.md` is the loomyard-owned `CONSTRAINTS.md`-equivalent,
and it lives in `weft` (see the `internal/boardengine` package documentation — "everything that isn't warp already lives in weft"), a separate repo reached through a junction into the warp worktree — so it is **already invisible to the Fabric repo's git history** simply by living there, with nothing extra to build.
This task therefore reduces to `CLAUDE.local.md` below.

## `CLAUDE.local.md` (a single file)

Loads alongside `CLAUDE.md`, additive.
Must physically exist in warp's working tree, so a directory junction doesn't apply directly:

- **Symlinks, not hard links.**
  Hard links are inode-based, not path-based — if whatever regenerates the source `CLAUDE.md` in weft uses the standard safe-write pattern (write to a temp file, atomic rename over the target), a hard link on the warp side keeps pointing at the *old* inode and silently stops reflecting updates.
  Symlinks are path-based and always resolve to whatever currently occupies the target path.
- **Windows note:** symlinks normally require admin, but Developer Mode (Settings → For Developers, Windows 10 1703+) grants `SeCreateSymbolicLinkPrivilege` to standard users without elevation — worth checking whether this can be enabled on managed/non-admin machines before assuming it's blocked.
- **Fallback if symlinks aren't available:** explicit re-link (or copy) at `loom` init time, not automatic filesystem-level linking.
  Accepts staleness only within a single run, not across runs — acceptable since `CLAUDE.md` content changes rarely mid-session.
- `CLAUDE.local.md` is **not** auto-gitignored by Claude Code — `loom`'s init step must explicitly ensure it's listed in warp's `.gitignore` (same mechanism already used for weft junctions).
- If warp already has its own pre-existing, committed `CLAUDE.md` (someone deliberately approved Claude's use in that repo), that's fine — `CLAUDE.local.md` loads alongside it and takes precedence on conflict, no special handling needed.

## Related

- The `internal/boardengine` package documentation and the shipped `PATTERN.md` — establish that `PATTERN.md`, the loomyard-owned `CONSTRAINTS.md`-equivalent, lives in `weft`, which supersedes this task's constraints-hiding half.
- `internal/fabricengine` — owned the junction re-pointing mechanism the now-superseded constraints-dir half would have reused (`CLAUDE.local.md` uses a symlink, not a junction).
- `internal/loomcli`'s session bootstrap — the init/session-bootstrap step that would trigger the symlink fallback and `.gitignore` entry for `CLAUDE.local.md`.

entries.title: Baseline producer and numerical-drift gate
entries.brief: Capture a before-state so a failure the task caused can be told from a pre-existing one; in numerical repos the failure to catch is drift
entries.body:
From `manifest/roadmap.md` Someday.
loomyard captures no before-state, so it cannot tell a pre-existing failure from one a task caused ([millhouse#1130](https://github.com/Knatte18/millhouse/issues/1130)).
In a numerical target repo (the drilling simulator) the failure to catch is drift, which an exit-code verdict like `plan.Verify`'s cannot express.

Agreed shape, not yet a design doc:
- A shared `Capture-Baseline` producer row right after `Preflight`, shared by reference the way `preflightshed` and `landingshed` share theirs, so the planner writes against the current numerical signature.
- The artifact lives in `.lyx/baseline/`, never `_lyx`: a numerical baseline is machine-bound (floating point, BLAS, compiler flags).
  Capture before the first edit, recompute after, compare, discard.
- Two seams, both owned by the target repo: `capture` (tree → artifact) and `compare` (before, after → verdict + findings, with per-channel tolerance).
  Loomyard owns the row, the seam shapes, and the artifact location.
- The gate rides `shuttleengine.GateSpec` on the `Webster` row; registering a validator name in `resolveGateSpec`'s switch is the unbuilt part.

Open:
- Whether compare runs once at Webster's exit (what `GateSpec` gives, since it fires at the Master run's finalize) or per batch (exact localization, a new batch-loop hook, N captures).
- A middle option: gate once, and localize by making the predicate of Webster's integration-stage `bisect` pluggable, at log₂(N) captures; bisect assumes monotone drift.
- A baseline tree whose capture itself fails should be recorded, not halt the run.

entries.body:
Operator 2026-10-04: the board needs an interactive view with filters, reachable without typing a lyx command each time.

- Rendering (operator, 2026-10-04: mechanical, never an LLM): `board.html` in `_board` is a fixed viewer, changed only when the viewer itself changes, with filters on kind, type and area labels, free-text search and expandable bodies.
  It loads a sibling `board-data.js` (`window.BOARD = {…}`), which lyx's Go code rewrites from `board.json` on every board write, committed in the same commit as README.md.
  A plain `fetch` of `board.json` does not work: browsers block it for a page opened from `file://`, while a `<script src>` loads.
  A working demo built on today's data was shown to the operator on 2026-10-04 (filters, grouping into Tasks/Bugs/Enhancements, expandable bodies, light and dark).
- Opening: `lyx ide` writes a VS Code task "Open board" into each worktree's VS Code config that opens `<hub>/_board/board.html` in the default browser, run from `Tasks: Run Task` or a keybinding; lyx resolves the path, so nothing is linked into the worktree and `PATTERN-hub-containment` holds.
  With Microsoft's Live Preview extension installed, the task may open it in a VS Code panel instead; VS Code alone shows HTML as source.
  A link from `_lyx` was considered and rejected: `_lyx` is the pair's weft, the board is hub-level, and file symlinks are not relied on (Windows).
- Phone: the board repo is private, so GitHub Pages needs a paid plan; instead make README.md easier to read in the GitHub app, grouped by type and area with collapsible `<details>` sections per area and per body.

Builds on `board-model`'s kind and labels.

entries.title: Discussion stage has no sanctioned path to land a repository edit ahead of Plan
entries.brief: Discussion has no sanctioned path to commit a PATTERN edit ahead of Plan
entries.body:
Imported from [issue #385](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/385).

During the Discussion stage of a loom task, the parent (`ly:orch`) relayed an operator request to edit `PATTERN.md` and `pattern/` directly in the task worktree, so the review rounds would read the revised rules.

The Discussion launch prompt allows only the two discussion files and no git.

entries.title: Shortcut commands built into lyx from one committed file
entries.brief: An embedded shortcut file, git-alias style: attach for reed attach, and one shortcut that starts the orch and attaches in the prime
entries.body:
Idea (operator, 2026-10-06): top-level shortcuts for the lyx commands the operator types most, declared in one simple file in this repo rather than as Go commands.

Examples:

- `attach` expands to `reed attach`.
- One shortcut for the prime runs `orch start`, then `reed attach`; the orch always runs in the prime.
  Name open: `spawn` was floated; `up` would read like `reed up`.
  It fits the decision recorded in task `bugfix-sessions` that start verbs never attach: the shortcut is where both happen, by naming `reed attach` explicitly.

## Shape (operator, 2026-10-06)

- The shortcuts are part of the deployed `lyx` binary, the same on every hub and repo: a committed file in the loomyard repo, embedded at build time (`go:embed`), never runtime config.
  No hub, repo or user can add or change one; changing a shortcut is a commit here and a deploy.
- The file maps a shortcut name to one lyx argv, or to a list of argvs run in order that stops at the first failure.
  Only lyx commands, never a shell string.
- At root construction lyx adds one cobra command per shortcut, in its own help group, whose `Short` names the expansion; running it re-dispatches the expanded args through the same root, so flags, envelopes and exit codes are the real command's.
  Extra args after the shortcut append to the last argv.
- A test fails when a shortcut names an existing command or another shortcut, or expands to a command that does not exist, so a broken file never builds into a binary that passes CI.

## Open

- Whether a shortcut may carry flags of its own or only append args.

More shortcuts get added here as the operator notices them.
Related notes: `ide-prime-setup` (a VS Code task that starts the orch) and `ide-reopen-prime` (reopen the prime window with one command).

entries.title: Who in a running task receives an instruction
entries.brief: Driver forwarding, an alias for the active strand kept by loom, or an on-call LLM per run: open for a brainstorm
entries.body:
Who in a running task receives an instruction from the orch or the operator, open for a brainstorm (operator, 2026-10-07).

Seen 2026-10-07: an operator decision about card 1 of `bugfix-sessions` arrived while Webster ran.
The orch has to know which agent owns the content at that moment (Discussion-Write, the plan agent, the Webster master, a Burler round) and message it, or fall back on a goto; mid-Webster no agent can change a begun card at all (`webster-amend-begun-card`).
The orch editing the run's files itself is never the answer.

Options raised:

- The driver forwards: it knows its current producer and the strand doing the work. One address per run, but an LLM relays in a turn of its own, may reword, and its stencil does not do this today.
- An alias such as `ly:<slug>:active` for the strand that owns the current step: deterministic, no LLM between.
  Creel must not know what runs or what is active (operator): it owns messages and injects only.
  So creel could at most store a plain name-to-name alias that loom itself sets at every producer transition, knowing nothing of its meaning; or the alias lives outside creel altogether.
- An on-call LLM per run, woken when an instruction needs judgment about the run (what a decision means for the plan, who must do what). The operator considered this before the driver existed, when the driver was a Go process; it rebuilds its context each time it wakes, and it adds a role.
- The driver itself becomes that on-call role, with read access to the plan: it already lives the whole run, but grows heavier than a step driver.

Plain routing ("deliver to whoever works now") and judgment ("what does this mean for the run") may want different answers.

Steps with no LLM at all: the Go producers (Preflight, Batchifier, the verify gates, Publish, Finalize, teardown) have no strand to deliver to.
A message could wait in its queue for the next LLM producer if the alias is resolved at delivery rather than at send, but that agent may not be the right one (after Batchifier comes the Webster master, while the instruction may concern the plan).
This suggests a split to discuss:
- Content ("the settle comes from config") goes into the decision record, which is durable, read by every later LLM producer, and needs no live receiver.
- Only an instruction that must act now needs a live receiver, and the most urgent one, stop, is a run pause (`lyx batten pause`), which works during a Go step too.

Operator leaning (2026-10-07): the driver takes the message.
It runs a Sonnet agent on purpose, to have judgment; it is the one LLM alive for the whole run, Go steps included, it knows where the run stands, and it receives messages while its `shed step` runs in the background.
With a message it could record content with `lyx loom decision add` (a lyx verb, not a source edit), forward it to the strand that owns the current step, or pause the run or ask for a goto.

Refined (operator, 2026-10-07): every instruction for a run is posted to its driver, which gets only the short reminder (sender and subject) and does not read the body by default.
Knowing which agent works now, it either reads it itself or forwards it with `lyx creel forward` (see the `creel` note), so the receiving agent talks to the original sender, not to the driver: a minimal routing job.

entries.title: Orch and batten: compact reload, one event-driven notice channel, a window per batten
entries.brief: The orch reloads as soon as compaction lands, batten sends one timely notice per state change without ticks, and each batten gets its own tmux window
entries.body:
The orch and batten side of a run's lifecycle: the orch reloads as soon as its compaction lands, it hears each state change once and on time, and it can see which batten runs it has in flight.

## Orch compact cycle times out before reload

A compact cycle never sees its own compaction finish, so it always waits out the handoff timeout and aborts.
Seen 2026-10-07 on the hub orch:

- 12:05:39 the watcher enters `compacting` and types `/compact`.
- 12:06:41 the compaction boundary is written to the transcript.
- 12:15:41 the phase ends with `last_abort_reason: "compaction timed out"`.
- The next idle turn end finds the boundary through the auto-compaction path (`CompactedSince`) and only then sends the reload, about ten minutes late.

Cause: `tickCompacting` (`internal/orchengine/watcher.go`) decides the compaction landed from the context reading of `st.ReadingTurnEnd`.
That field is written only in the idle phase (the `st.Phase == PhaseIdle && isTurnEnd(ev)` branch of the tick's event read), never while the phase is `compacting`.
So it stays on the turn end from before `/compact`, whose reading can never show `Compacted`, and the turn ends after the compaction are not read.

Side effects:

- The cycle counts as aborted: `cycle_count` does not move and `last_deferral` is set, which can push back the next automatic cycle.
- A `distill` request queued during the cycle is removed as stale (`orch: stale cycle request removed`) instead of being acted on.

Fix direction: in `compacting`, take each turn end read after the phase entry as the reading candidate, or ask the transcript for a boundary after `PhaseEnteredAt` directly, as the auto path does.
A test drives a compact cycle through a turn end that follows the boundary and asserts the reload starts without the timeout.

## One notice channel to the orch

Seen 2026-10-06: the orch gets two messages for every halt, and the batten one is often stale.

- The driver messages the orch at once with its stop report.
- Batten's Run-Shed row polls the child only every `poll_interval_s: 30` (`contracts/recipes/batten-recipe.yaml`), so its `[batten notice]` lags up to half a minute.
- The notice is typed into the orch pane and read only when the orch's current turn ends; by then the orch has often resumed the run, and the notice reports a state that no longer holds (twice on 2026-10-06: "paused" and "awaiting" for runs already running again; on 2026-10-07 most notices of the day were stale on arrival).

Direction:

- One channel per event: batten owns state changes (blocked, paused, awaiting PR-Gate, done) and its notice carries the drive report path; the driver messages the orch only with a question it cannot settle itself, never with "the run stopped".
  Parent-review requests and escalation briefs keep coming from the producer session.
- The notice is event-driven, not polled: batten wakes on the child's status-file change (or polls at a few seconds), since the orch relies on it as its only wake-up.
- Batten has no ticks (operator, 2026-10-07): the wait on the child is one step that blocks until the child's state changes, not a Run-Shed row that bounces `stuck` every 30 s.
  Batten's history records only the child's state changes, each with its timestamp; today every bounce adds a history entry (83 entries for `test-tiers` within an hour, all `Run-Shed → stuck`), which is noise, not history.
- The quiet notice measures the wrong thing: it fires when the child's status file is unchanged for 45 min, but the status file changes only at a step's end, so a live agent working a long step, or one already resumed, still trips it.
  On 2026-10-07 all five runs stalled on an API error; the quiet notices arrived 45 min later, long after the agents were resumed by hand, and said nothing about the cause.
  Quiet should be judged from the agent's own activity (transcript growth, turn ends) and should name an API-error turn end when that is what it sees.
- Each notice carries the time the state held and the child's history length, so a stale notice is recognisable without a status call.

## A window per batten

Seen 2026-10-03: the hub orch starts each batten detached with `setsid nohup lyx batten run <slug>`, so nothing on screen shows what the orch has running; Claude Code's footer shows only "1 shell" for a background helper, which says nothing about what it does.
Idea (operator): when the orch starts a batten, it lands in its own tmux window in the orch's session, so the window list names every run the orch has in flight.
`manifest/designs/reed-multi-window.md` sketches reed's own-window anchoring.

Related notes, not in this task: `orch-owns-the-loop` (lyx starts batten detached, a lyx watch, one land command) and `runs-overview` (one status line per run, the event log in its own window).
